div.head: Episc 13
div.ab: Hit bið ælces hlafordes agen þearf, þæt he his nydþeowum byrge, swa he betst mæge, for ðam þe hy syn Gode efen leofe ⁊ þa ðe syndon freolse, ⁊ us ealle he gebohte mid gelican weorðe.

Uniuscuiusque domini proprium est necesse, ut seruis suis (compatiatur et) condescendat, sicut melius (indulgentius) poterit; quia domino Deo (uiuenti) sunt eque cari seruus et liber, et omnes redemit uno (eodem) precio.
Hit bið ælces hlafordes agen þearf þæt he his nydþeowum byrge swa he betst mæge, for ðam þe hy syn Gode efen leofe and þa ðe syndon freolse, and us ealle he gebohte mid gelican weorðe.

Es ist jedes Herrn eigener Nutzen, dass er seinen Sklaven Schonung gewähre, wie er bestens kann, weil sie Gott ebenso lieb sind [Sklav und Quadr.] wie die die frei sind, und uns alle erkaufte er [erlöste Christus] mit gleichem Preise.

It is every lord's own interest that he spare his slaves as best he can, because they are as dear to God [slave and, Quadr.] as those who are free, and he [Christ the Redeemer] bought us all with the same price.
It is the responsibility of every master to protect his slaves as best he can, for they are loved by God as much as those who are free, and he bought us all for the same price.
div.note: 13–15 are similar to a homily attributed to Wulfstan (ed. Napier 300), in a less fitting context and so not the source, Liebermann thinks. Liebermann compares 10.
slaves: Old English nidþeowum, literally “slaves by compulsion,” that is, those who have entered slavery because of poverty or starvation.
